extensions.name: improv
extensions.description: Improv's spreadsheet formula language (681 functions) and multidimensional models (categories, measures, formulas over them) on DuckDB tables

docs.hello_world:
LOAD improv;
-- Any of Improv's 681 built-in functions, on named inputs.
SELECT improv_calc('ROUND(PMT(rate/12, n, -pv), 2)',
                   json_object('rate', 0.06, 'n', 360, 'pv', 200000));  -- 1199.1
SELECT improv_calc_text('1/0');                                          -- #DIV/0!
SELECT name, signature FROM improv_functions(query := 'pmt');
-- A multidimensional model over a table: one row per computed cell.
CREATE TABLE sales AS SELECT * FROM (VALUES
  (2024, 'WidgetA', 10, 100), (2024, 'WidgetB', 20, 50),
  (2025, 'WidgetA', 11, 120), (2025, 'WidgetB', 20, 40)) t(year, product, price, qty);
SELECT * FROM improv('sales', '
  category Time = year
  category Product = product
  input Price = price
  input Quantity = qty sum
  Revenue = Price * Quantity
  Share = Revenue / SUM(Revenue OVER Product)
  Growth = Revenue - PREV(Revenue, Time, 1, 0)');
docs.extended_description:
Improv is a multidimensional spreadsheet in the Lotus Improv / Quantrix
tradition: data lives in categories (Time, Product, Region) instead of
cell addresses, and formulas name measures (`Revenue = Price *
Quantity`), so one formula covers every cell it applies to.

This extension brings its formula engine to DuckDB:

- `improv_calc(formula [, inputs])` evaluates a scalar Improv formula
  (math, statistics, financial, text, dates, engineering, `IF`, `LET`,
  `LAMBDA`; aggregations over categories need a model) on named inputs
  passed as a JSON object. An error value is NULL; `improv_calc_text`
  returns any type and renders errors (`#DIV/0!`).
- `improv_functions([query := ...])` lists the functions with their
  signatures and descriptions.
- `improv(source, model)` reads a table or a SELECT, builds a model from
  a short spec (categories from columns, inputs from columns with an
  optional sum/avg/min/max/count, derived measures as formulas, with
  aggregations across categories and PREV/NEXT along them) and returns
  one row per computed cell, ready to join.

The same engine runs Improv's desktop GUI, terminal UI, CLI and its
PostgreSQL extension (pg_improv). Source: https://codeberg.org/gregburd/improv

extensions.name: ivf
extensions.description: OSA Levenshtein + Meilisearch-style typo tolerance for FTS (ivf_levenshtein, transposition = 1), with an exact-recall IVF-Flat vector baseline

docs.extended_description:
## ivf — OSA Levenshtein + typo tolerance for DuckDB FTS

Pure-Rust (zero non-std dependencies), C-API v1.2.0. Two capability
groups:

**1. `ivf_levenshtein(a, b[, maxd])` — OSA Damerau-Levenshtein.**
An adjacent transposition counts as ONE edit (the dominant class of real
keyboard typos; plain Levenshtein counts 2) — the same semantics
Meilisearch uses for typo tolerance. Banded with early exit, optional
`maxd` saturation.

On top of the official `fts` extension (DuckDB >= 2.0) this powers a
SQL macro layer (`test/fts_typo.sql`, load with `CREATE MACRO` from the
file) implementing Meilisearch-style search: length-tiered edit budgets
(<=3 letters never corrected, 4-5 tolerate 1, 6+ tolerate 2), correction
against the fts `raw_dict` (surface forms), two-way `synonyms` that
outrank typo correction, and an **expand-not-replace** entry point —
the original and corrected queries both run and are fused, so a wrong
correction can never hurt recall. Measured on 120k ag_news headlines
(bge-m3 vectors, 50 single-typo queries): nDCG@10 0.657 (no correction)
-> 0.705 (expand) -> 0.909 with vector fusion; word-level correction
recall 13/50 (the ceiling is the corpus dictionary — names/new words
are OOV).

**2. IVF-Flat vector index — exact-recall baseline.**
`ivf_create_index` / `ivf_search` (nprobe) / `ivf_search_exact`
(brute force) / `ivf_list`. Positioning: a dependency-free,
uncompressed exact-recall control for eval harnesses and
ground-truth checks — not a competitive ANN engine (see official `vss`
for HNSW, `vindex`/turbovec for quantized ANN).

**Platforms:** Linux x64, macOS arm64/x64, Windows x64 (CI-built).
Load with `INSTALL ivf FROM community;` (or `LOAD 'ivf.duckdb_extension'`
with `-unsigned` for local builds).

extensions.name: jasp_ext
extensions.description: Read JASP project files (.jasp) as SQL tables — data, column metadata and analysis registry

docs.extended_description:
The jasp_ext extension reads [JASP](https://www.jasp.org/) project files (`.jasp`) directly as SQL tables.

A `.jasp` file is a ZIP archive containing `internal.sqlite` (the real data), `analyses.json`
(analysis registry) and `resources/N/jaspResults.json` (per-analysis results). Data lives in
`DataSet` / `DataSet_N` tables where every logical column is stored as a pair of physical
columns (`Column_{id}_DBL` value, `Column_{id}_INT` categorical code). The extension maps
these back to logical typed columns:

| JASP column type | DuckDB type | source |
|---|---|---|
| scale | DOUBLE | `_DBL` REAL value, `nan` → NULL |
| ordinal | DOUBLE | `_DBL` code |
| nominal | VARCHAR | `Labels[_INT]` |
| nominalText | VARCHAR | `_DBL` text value |

**Table functions:**

| function | description |
|---|---|
| `read_jasp(path)` | all data rows (typed), from the default DataSet |
| `read_jasp(path, dataset)` | a specific `DataSet_N` |
| `read_jasp_columns(path [, dataset])` | column metadata (id, name, columnType) |
| `read_jasp_analyses(path)` | one row per registered analysis |

**Example:**

```sql
SELECT * FROM read_jasp('/path/to/project.jasp');
SELECT * FROM read_jasp_columns('/path/to/project.jasp');
SELECT * FROM read_jasp_analyses('/path/to/project.jasp');
```

**Install:** `INSTALL jasp_ext FROM community;`

**Source:** [alitrack/duckdb_jasp](https://github.com/alitrack/duckdb_jasp)

extensions.name: lakemon
extensions.description: Smart DuckLake table maintain (adaptive rewrite + merge) and catalog-global expire/cleanup

docs.extended_description:
lakemon orchestrates native DuckLake maintenance CALLs with a policy layer:

* Catalog SELECT inventory of data files, delete files, and inlined-delete backlog
* Flush guard (lakemon_flush_inlined_max_delete_files) so a large ended-file delete backlog cannot block rewrite/merge
* Byte-weighted adaptive rewrite ladder (delete fraction DESC; one ducklake_rewrite_data_files CALL per byte-cut rung)
* Merge size bands (micro / small / medium) with per-tier target_file_size
* Table maintain (lakemon_maintain) vs catalog-global expire/cleanup (lakemon_maintain_global)
* CALL / SELECT plan and execute by default (dry_run for plan only)
* One result row per step (ok / skip / error / planned)
* Optional stderr step logs with duration and byte-weighted progress

Requires the core ducklake extension in the same session and an attached DuckLake catalog.
Compatible with DuckDB 1.5.6 and DuckDB 2.0.0 (lakemon 0.2.0+). Older DuckDB 1.5.x builds are no longer produced.

extensions.name: laterite_ags4
extensions.description: Read AGS4 geotechnical data files as typed, UUID-keyed tables directly from SQL — born-typed columns, deterministic content-addressed keys that join across groups by construction, and an embedded AGS dictionary. A read-only SQL surface. Local, http(s):// and s3:// (with httpfs).

docs.extended_description:
`laterite_ags4` reads [AGS4](https://www.ags.org.uk/) geotechnical & geoenvironmental
data files as first-class DuckDB tables — no conversion step, no bundled engine.

Written in 🦀 Rust on DuckDB's C Extension API (zero C++). Part of the
[laterite](https://docs.laterite.dev/) toolkit and, like the rest of it,
**in beta** — see [what beta means](https://docs.laterite.dev/reference/support/).

### What it gives you

- **Born-typed columns** — each heading is typed from the file's own `TYPE` row
  (`2DP` → `DOUBLE`, `ID` → `VARCHAR`, `0DP` → `BIGINT`, `YN` → `BOOLEAN`, …).
- **Deterministic content-addressed keys** — every row carries `_id` and
  `_parent_id` (UUIDv8 of the row's spec key-chain). `child._parent_id == parent._id`
  **by construction**, so groups join across independent `read_ags(...)` calls with
  no shared state.
- **Self-describing metadata** — `ags_groups`, `ags_headings`, `ags_dictionary`,
  `ags_relationships` expose the file's structure and the embedded AGS dictionary.
- **Persistence** — `load_ags(path)` emits CREATE-TABLE DDL for an indexed,
  repeat-/remote-query store.
- **Local or remote** — reads go through DuckDB's virtual filesystem, so local paths,
  `http(s)://` and `s3://` (with `LOAD httpfs`) all work on one code path.
- **Native + wasm** — built for the community-extensions native platforms and
  DuckDB-WASM (`wasm_mvp`, `wasm_eh`): the same reader for native and browser DuckDB.

### Functions

| function | returns |
|---|---|
| `read_ags(path, group)` | one group as a typed table — `_id`, `_parent_id`, then one column per heading (typed from the file's `TYPE` row). Reads local / `http(s)://` / `s3://`. |
| `read_ags_text(content, group)` | the same typed table, from an **inline AGS4 string** (no filesystem). |
| `ags_groups(path)` | `(group, n_rows, n_headings, parent)` — the file's group list. |
| `ags_headings(path)` | `(group, heading, unit, ags_type, sql_type, status, is_key, ordinal)` — the per-heading schema, enriched with the dictionary's KEY status. |
| `ags_dictionary()` | the embedded standard AGS dictionary as a table (`group`, `heading`, `status`, `ags_type`, `unit`, `description`, …). |
| `ags_relationships()` | `(child, parent, shared_keys)` — the spec parent→child graph that `_parent_id` follows. |
| `ags_rules()` | the AGS4 numbered-rule catalogue (`rule`, `title`, `severity`, `fixable`) — the extension *lists* the rules; the CLI/library *run* them. |
| `load_ags(path)` | `(seq, stmt)` — CREATE-TABLE DDL to materialise every group into an indexed, repeat-/remote-queryable store. |

Readers stream lazily (≈2048-row vector chunks); a non-conforming numeric cell becomes
`NULL`, never an error (the born-typed behaviour). Optional arguments are **named**
(`edition := '4.2'`, `encoding := 'windows-1252'`), the rest positional. The path verbs
take an `encoding` named param (e.g. `encoding := 'windows-1252'`) for non-UTF-8
sources; the `_text` variant is UTF-8 (its input is already a `VARCHAR`). This is a
**read-only SQL surface** — validation, certification and repair stay in the `lat`
CLI / the `laterite` library.

extensions.name: loki
extensions.description: Query Grafana Loki from DuckDB in plain SQL, with label/time/line-filter pushdown into LogQL

docs.extended_description:
`loki` turns a Grafana Loki instance into a first-class, queryable DuckDB data
source, so you can join your logs against Parquet, CSV, Postgres, or anything
else DuckDB reads — without ever hand-writing an HTTP request.

- **`loki(selector := ...)`** — pushdown-driven. SQL `WHERE` filters on promoted
  label columns, `timestamp`, and `line` are translated into the LogQL stream
  selector, `start`/`end` time bounds, and line filters. Untranslatable predicates
  are left as residuals for DuckDB to apply, so results are always correct.
- **`loki_scan(query := ...)`** — a raw-LogQL escape hatch for full control.
- **`loki_labels()` / `loki_label_values()` / `loki_series()`** — label discovery
  helpers so the source is explorable and autocompletes well.
- **`ATTACH '...' AS lk (TYPE loki)`** — Loki as a read-only attached database:
  `lk.<tenant>.logs` (plus `labels` and `series`) with the same pushdown, label
  columns auto-discovered at attach time and refreshable via
  `PRAGMA loki_refresh_labels`. Because Loki refuses a query without a stream
  selector, a scan of `logs` must carry a `WHERE` on at least one label column.

Connection and auth (bearer token, basic auth, `X-Scope-OrgID` tenant, or arbitrary
headers) come from DuckDB's Secret Manager with per-call overrides. A
`CREATE SECRET (TYPE loki, PROVIDER env)` seeds the connection from the standard
logcli environment variables (`LOKI_ADDR`, `LOKI_BEARER_TOKEN`,
`LOKI_USERNAME`/`LOKI_PASSWORD`, `LOKI_ORG_ID`), with inline options overriding the
environment. Results page
automatically over Loki's per-request entry cap, and projection pushdown skips
materialising the columns a query doesn't select. Timestamps keep Loki's nanosecond
resolution (`TIMESTAMP_NS`). See the
[repository](https://github.com/prochac/duckdb-loki) for full documentation.

extensions.name: luajit
extensions.description: In-process LuaJIT UDFs for DuckDB — JIT-compiled, parallel (per-thread states), trusted sandbox, GROUP BY aggregates, LIST/STRUCT/MAP bridges, embedded Fennel compiler

docs.extended_description:
## luajit — JIT-compiled Lua UDFs for DuckDB

Write and run Lua functions directly in SQL. LuaJIT compiles them to native machine
code with trace-based JIT, with **parallel execution**: each DuckDB worker thread
owns its own lua_State (no global lock), so thread parallelism maps directly to
LuaJIT parallelism.

**16 Functions:**
- `luajit_i` / `luajit_f` / `luajit_b` — typed scalar UDFs (BIGINT, DOUBLE, BOOLEAN)
- `luajit_v` / `luajit_vi` / `luajit_vs` — **chunk-batched scalar** (1 Lua call per chunk, ~1.9× row-mode)
- `luajit_m` — mixed-type auto-cast
- `luajit_l` / `luajit_s` / `luajit_map` — LIST/STRUCT/MAP type bridges (nested types incl. DATE)
- `luajit_agg` — aggregate UDFs with GROUP BY support (per-group full value table)
- `luajit_table` — streaming table-generating UDFs (O(1) memory, 1M rows)
- `luajit_module` — module management (**14 modes**: compile, quick_compile, fennel, trusted, inspect, macro, list, drop, reset, save, load, last_error, info)

**Features:**
- **Auto-detection (v0.23)**: quick_compile probes the UDF (int/date/STRUCT/array)
  and auto-generates the right scalar or batch macro — no manual style selection
- **Per-thread lua_State pool (P4)**: no global lock on Lua execution — DuckDB
  parallelism → LuaJIT parallelism (~2.6× on 4 threads, CPU-bound UDFs)
- **trusted sandbox mode**: removes io/ffi/package/require/load*/debug, reduces os
  (applies lazily per state, on/off across threads)
- **`_duckdb_query` bridge**: run SQL from Lua, get result sets as Lua tables
- **Embedded Fennel compiler** (`mode:='fennel'`): Lisp syntax (match patterns,
  compile-time macros) compiled to Lua — zero runtime cost
- DATE/TIMESTAMP/DECIMAL/HUGEINT bridging (incl. int64/int128 decimal storage)
- GROUP BY aggregates with full value tables (median, stddev, percentile, …)
- GC64 build: no 2GB memory ceiling; ~1MB self-contained binary, zero runtime deps
- save/load persistence with multi-line source escaping

**Performance (1M rows, 2 BIGINT args, `a*b+a`, 4 threads):**
- batch `luajit_vi`: 13ms; row `luajit_i`: 13ms (2.6× vs row+serial)
- single-thread: batch 18ms (1.9× row-mode 34ms)

**Platforms:** Linux x64/arm64, Windows (MSVC), macOS x64/arm64. WASM and mingw/rtools
excluded (LuaJIT requires specific toolchains); linux_arm64 verified (v0.31, CI + arm64 runtime test).

extensions.name: marc21
extensions.description: Read, write, validate and edit MARC 21 bibliographic data (ISO 2709, MARCXML, MARC-in-JSON, breaker, Aleph; UTF-8 and MARC-8)

docs.extended_description:
A cleanly licensed MARC 21 toolkit for DuckDB, aimed at cataloging and
metadata librarians: the parser, MARC-8 tables and writer are implemented
from ISO 2709 and the Library of Congress specifications only, not from
previous software, and verified by differential fuzzing and round-trip
testing.

### Read
`read_marc` (nested LIST(STRUCT) per record), `read_marc_subfields`
(one row per subfield), `read_marc_raw` (original bytes + error column),
`read_marcxml`, `read_marc_breaker`, `read_marcjson` (community shape,
NDJSON and FOLIO SRS envelopes), `read_alephseq`.  Glob patterns, gzip,
and DuckDB FileSystem protocols (httpfs URLs — including SRU and OAI-PMH
responses, whose envelopes are handled).  `read_z3950` retrieves records
live from Z39.50 servers (Library of Congress, OCLC, most ILSes) with a
built-in dependency-free client.  On DuckDB v2.0 the readers are
multi-file readers (lists of paths, `filename` and `file_index` columns,
`union_by_name`, `hive_partitioning`, parallel across files).  Scans
parallelise across and within files.

### Write
`COPY ... TO (FORMAT marc | marcxml | mrk | marcjson)`.  ISO 2709 output
in UTF-8 or MARC-8 (full LC code tables: ANSEL, Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew,
Arabic, EACC with escape designations; NCR fallback), round-trip tested.

### Query, validate, edit
MARCspec addressing (`marc_spec`), structural and Avram-schema validation
(`marc_validate`, `marc_validate_avram`), format detection, record
editing (`marc_set_subfield`, `marc_remove_fields`, `marc_replace_values`,
...), merge with field protection (`marc_merge`), record diff
(`marc_diff`), identifier normalisation (`marc_isbn13`, `marc_issn`,
`marc_lccn`, `marc_oclc`), NACO normalisation and match keys for
deduplication, and a FOLIO Source Record Storage bridge
(`marc_parse_json`) for in-place analytics on an ATTACHed FOLIO database.

extensions.name: markdown
extensions.description: Read, analyze, and write Markdown files with block-level document representation and inline element support

docs.extended_description:
The Markdown extension adds comprehensive Markdown processing capabilities to DuckDB, enabling structured analysis, transformation, and generation of Markdown documents.

**Documentation:** [https://duckdb-markdown.readthedocs.io/](https://duckdb-markdown.readthedocs.io/)

**Key Features:**

- **File Reading Functions**: Read Markdown files with `read_markdown()`, `read_markdown_sections()`, and `read_markdown_blocks()` supporting glob patterns, metadata extraction, and block-level parsing
- **Block-Level Representation**: Parse documents into duck_block format with `kind` (block/inline), `element_type`, `content`, `level`, `encoding`, `attributes`, and `element_order` columns
- **Inline Element Support**: Build rich text content with bold, italic, links, code, math, and more using the unified duck_block structure
- **COPY TO Markdown**: Export query results as Markdown tables, documents, or block-level representations with full round-trip support
- **Content Extraction**: Extract code blocks, links, images, and tables from Markdown content using structured LIST<STRUCT> return types
- **Document Processing**: Convert markdown to HTML/text, validate content, extract metadata, and generate document statistics
- **Replacement Scan Support**: Query Markdown files directly using `FROM '*.md'` syntax with full glob pattern support
- **Native MARKDOWN Type**: Custom MARKDOWN type with automatic VARCHAR casting for seamless integration
- **Cross-Platform Support**: Works on Linux, macOS, WebAssembly, and Windows
- **GitHub Flavored Markdown**: Uses cmark-gfm for accurate parsing of modern Markdown features
- **High Performance**: Process thousands of documents efficiently with 4,000+ sections/second processing rate

**Core Functions:**

- `read_markdown()` - Read Markdown files with comprehensive parameter support
- `read_markdown_sections()` - Parse files into hierarchical sections with filtering options
- `read_markdown_blocks()` - Parse files into block-level elements (duck_block shape)
- `duck_block_to_md()` - Convert single block/inline element to Markdown
- `duck_blocks_to_md()` - Convert list of elements to Markdown document
- `duck_blocks_to_sections()` - Convert blocks to hierarchical sections
- `md_extract_code_blocks()` - Extract code blocks with language and metadata
- `md_extract_links()` - Extract links with text, URL, and title information
- `md_extract_images()` - Extract images with alt text and metadata
- `md_extract_tables_json()` - Extract tables as structured JSON
- `md_to_html()` - Convert markdown content to HTML
- `md_to_text()` - Convert markdown to plain text for full-text search
- `md_stats()` - Get document statistics (word count, reading time, etc.)
- `md_extract_metadata()` - Extract frontmatter metadata as MAP

**COPY TO Modes:**

- `table` (default) - Export any query as a formatted Markdown table
- `document` - Reconstruct Markdown from sections with headings and content
- `blocks` / `duck_block` - Round-trip block-level representation with inline element support

**Example Use Cases:**

- Documentation analysis across entire repositories
- Content quality assessment and auditing
- Large-scale documentation search and indexing
- Code example extraction and analysis
- Document transformation pipelines
- Rich text generation with inline formatting
- Knowledge base processing and content management

**Performance:**

Real-world benchmark: Processing 287 Markdown files (2,699 sections, 1,137 code blocks, 1,174 links) in 603ms.

Full test suite with 2058 passing assertions across 60 test files.

extensions.name: maxmind
extensions.description: Read MaxMind databases (GeoLite, GeoIP, and more)

docs.hello_world: SELECT geolite_city('./GeoLite2-City.mmdb', '1.0.64.0', '');
docs.extended_description:
Read any MaxMind database using table and scalar functions.
GeoLite and GeoIP databases get typed columns;
other MMDB files return a `record` JSON column.

Scan all IP network blocks with `read_mmdb()`.
Use the optional `network` parameter to limit the scan to a subnet,
e.g., `read_mmdb(path, network='1.0.0.0/8')`.
Empty records are excluded by default; use `include_empty=true` to include them.

```sql
SELECT network, city.names.en
FROM read_mmdb('./GeoLite2-City.mmdb')
WHERE city.names.en IS NOT NULL
LIMIT 1;
┌─────────────┬───────────┐
│   network   │    en     │
├─────────────┼───────────┤
│ 1.0.64.0/20 │ Hiroshima │
└─────────────┴───────────┘
```

Look up a record by IP address with typed scalar functions that return structs.
The third parameter filters which fields to decode for faster lookups (pass `''` for all fields).

```sql
SELECT geolite_city('./GeoLite2-City.mmdb', '1.0.64.0', 'city').city.names.en AS en;
┌───────────┐
│    en     │
├───────────┤
│ Hiroshima │
└───────────┘
```

Use `mmdb_record()` to look up a record from any MMDB file as JSON:

```sql
SELECT mmdb_record('./GeoLite2-City.mmdb', '1.0.64.0', 'city') -> 'city' -> 'names' ->> 'en' AS en;
┌───────────┐
│    en     │
├───────────┤
│ Hiroshima │
└───────────┘
```

extensions.name: mentat
extensions.description: Datomic-compatible Datalog query engine as a DuckDB extension

docs.extended_description:
mentat is a Datomic-compatible database: an EDN/Datalog front-end over an
entity-attribute-value store with history. This extension stores mentat's
datoms in DuckDB: each mentat store is a schema of ordinary tables in the
database the extension is loaded into, so the data persists with that
database and plain SQL can read it. It exposes `edn_t` (transact), `edn_q`
(Datalog query table function, with :in inputs and asOf/since), `edn_pull`
(pull pattern -> JSON) and `edn_eval` (sandboxed mino script), so Datalog
query results can be joined against native DuckDB tables. The same engine is also
available as an embedded Rust library and CLI (on SQLite) and a PostgreSQL
extension (`pg_mentat`). Source: https://codeberg.org/gregburd/mentat

extensions.name: midi
extensions.description: Read, analyze, generate, and play MIDI files with SQL. Provides table functions for parsing Standard MIDI Files, scalar functions for note/frequency conversion, and macOS playback via AudioToolbox.

docs.extended_description:
duckdb-midi brings MIDI file support to DuckDB. Parse, analyze, generate, and play
Standard MIDI Files entirely from SQL.

**Table Functions**:
- `read_midi(path)` - All MIDI events as a table (note_on, note_off, control_change, meta, etc.)
- `midi_notes(path)` - Note-on/off pairs with duration, velocity, and note name
- `midi_meta(path)` - Meta events (tempo, time signature, key signature, track names)

**Scalar Functions**:
- `midi_note_name(60)` → `'C4'`
- `midi_note_number('C4')` → `60`
- `midi_note_freq(69)` → `440.0`
- `midi_bpm_to_uspqn(120.0)` → `500000`
- `midi_uspqn_to_bpm(500000)` → `120.0`

**Write / Generate**:
- `midi_write(path, notes[], durations[], velocities[], bpm)` - Create MIDI from arrays
- `midi_gen(path, preset)` - Generate test MIDI (scale, chord, arpeggio, drum, chromatic)

**Playback (macOS)**:
- `midi_play(path)` - Play MIDI file (blocks until finished)
- `midi_stop()` - Stop playback

Uses [craigsapp/midifile](https://github.com/craigsapp/midifile) for SMF parsing/writing
and macOS AudioToolbox for playback.

extensions.name: miniplot
extensions.description: SQL-driven interactive charts, narrative HTML reports, and optional native PNG/PDF export

docs.extended_description:
Interactive visualization from DuckDB SQL using Plotly.js. Includes bar, line,
area, scatter, 3D scatter, histogram, box, pie, donut, horizontal bar, violin,
bubble, heatmap, contour, step, radar, and WebGL scatter charts. Numeric and
date/time axes preserve numeric spacing and UTC handling for zoned timestamps.

HTML-returning functions work without file writes or browser launches. Native
file/browser functions support temporary or explicit output paths and respect
DuckDB's external-access setting. Plotly.js is loaded from a CDN for ordinary
HTML viewing; a browser connection or cached bundle is needed.

Narrative reports accept a documented JSON specification (title and sections
containing escaped prose plus optional Plotly data/layout/config). Reports
retain their non-executable JSON specification for agent workflows and
reproducibility. Function signatures, descriptions and examples are available
through duckdb_functions().

Optional chart_export(html, output_path) creates PNG or PDF on a native host.
This requires a separately installed local Node.js/Playwright/Chromium tool and
MINIPLOT_EXPORTER pointing to scripts/export-chart.cjs from the source checkout.
It uses the installed local Plotly bundle without network requests. These tools
are not bundled in the community extension. Wasm users should use HTML output;
Wasm cannot spawn the local exporter.

WebGL scatter supports large point sets without silently sampling data, subject
to browser/GPU memory limits. Array values must be finite and non-NULL, with
documented length and grid-shape validation. Measured serialization results,
report JSON schema, source-build instructions and export setup are in the
repository README and docs directory.

extensions.name: ml
extensions.description: Lightweight, columnar-native ML for DuckDB — train + inference, 34 algorithms, zero Python deps

docs.extended_description:
## ML — Machine Learning for DuckDB

Pure Rust ML extension. 34 algorithms, zero Python dependencies.

**Algorithms (34):**
- Regression: linear_regression, ridge_regression, lasso_regression, elastic_net, robust (Huber), polynomial_regression

extensions.name: mlpack
extensions.description: Connecting duckdb to the mlpack C++ machine learning library

docs.extended_description:
### Supervised Learning
The mlpack extension allows to fit (or train) and predict (or classify) from the models implemented, currently adaBoost, Bayesian linear regression, decision tree, LARS, linear regression,
logistic regression, naive Bayes, random forests as well as softmax regression.
The format is the same for these methods: four tables, say, "X", "Y", "Z" and "M" provide input for, respectively, features "X", labels "Y", optional parameters varying by model in "Z" as well as an output table "M" for the JSON-serialized model.
For all methods, following a model fit (or training), a prediction (or classification) can be made using "M" and new predictor values "N" as shown in the example.
All these "fit" (or "train") methods take four parameter tables, all "predict" methods take two.

### Unsupervised Learning
A kMeans clustering method is also available.
It uses three tables for data, parameters and results.

### General Information
A pair of parameters "mlpack_verbose" (to show additional data) and "mlpack_silent" (to suppress display of minimal summaries) can also be set.

The implementation is wraps several supervised and unsupervised machine learning methods, and provides Linux and macOS builds.
More methods, options or parameters can be added quite easily.

For more, please see the [repo](https://github.com/eddelbuettel/duckdb-mlpack).

extensions.name: mmcif
extensions.description: Read and write protein structure mmcif files using SQL

extensions.name: mongo
extensions.description: Integrates DuckDB with MongoDB, enabling direct SQL queries and writes over MongoDB collections without ETL

docs.extended_description:
The duckdb-mongo extension provides direct SQL access to MongoDB collections without requiring data export
or ETL processes. It supports both standalone MongoDB instances and MongoDB Atlas clusters.

**Reading data:**
- Automatic schema inference from sampled documents, with nested document flattening
- User-provided schemas and Atlas SQL `__schema` document support
- Query pushdown to MongoDB for filters (including struct field predicates), projections, limits, TopN, and aggregations (COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX, AVG)
- `VARIANT` columns that keep each value's own BSON type: opt-in per column, as the inference fallback (`nested_type := 'variant'`), or for whole documents (`raw := true`), with path projection and predicate pushdown
- `mongo_sample_size` setting to control schema inference sampling
- `MongoQuery` log type to inspect the exact commands sent to MongoDB
- BSON type mapping including ObjectId, Decimal128, arrays, and nested documents

**Writing data:**
- `INSERT INTO` -- insert rows from any DuckDB source (CSV, Parquet, other databases, subqueries)
- `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` -- create new MongoDB collections from query results
- `COPY TO (FORMAT mongo)` -- bulk-load data into MongoDB collections
- `DROP TABLE` -- drop MongoDB collections

**Connections and security:**
- MongoDB Atlas support via connection strings or DuckDB Secrets, including arbitrary URI options (e.g. `readPreference`) via the secret's `OPTIONS` key
- TLS/SSL encryption, custom CA certificates
- `mongo_enable_direct_scan` setting to restrict `mongo_scan` to attached catalogs only

For detailed setup and usage instructions, visit the [extension repository](https://github.com/stephaniewang526/duckdb-mongo).

extensions.name: motorsport_telemetry
extensions.description: Query AiM MP4, Cosworth PDS, MoTeC LD, Racelogic VBOX and .telemetry recordings directly in DuckDB, with stint-aware laps

docs.hello_world:
SELECT name, unit, frequency_hz, sample_count
FROM telemetry_metadata('run.ld')
WHERE sample_count > 0;

SELECT *
FROM read_telemetry('run.ld',
  rate := 100,
  channels := 'Ground Speed,Throttle Pos,Brake Pedal Pos');

SELECT name, unit, frequency_hz, sample_count
FROM telemetry_metadata('run.mp4')
WHERE sample_count > 0;

SELECT *
FROM read_aim('run.mp4',
  rate := 10,
  channels := 'RPM,GPS Speed,GPS Latitude,GPS Longitude');
docs.extended_description:
`motorsport_telemetry` reads AiM `aimd` telemetry embedded in MP4, Pi
Research/Cosworth PDS, MoTeC i2 LD, Racelogic VBOX VBO, and
motorsport-telemetry-rs `.telemetry` recordings (zstd-compressed MTJ JSONL) without an export step.
`telemetry_laps` returns each lap with a session-monotonic virtual lap
number, stint index, the dash's own stint lap counter, and a normalized
kind (flying, out, in, out-in, pit); `telemetry_file_metadata` reports
flying-lap and stint counts and picks the fastest flying lap. AiM MP4 support is native-only; the DuckDB-Wasm build does not
link the AiM parser, so `.mp4` inputs and the `read_aim`/`read_aimd`
functions are unavailable in the browser. The native reader exposes scalar
`CHS` channels and expands each valid 56-byte `GPS0` aggregate into 16 GPS
channels, including WGS84 position, speed, heading, accuracy, timing, and
status. It provides exact channel metadata, native-rate long-form samples,
and projected wide readers with time/channel pruning and type-aware
interpolation. Integer and event channels always use previous-value
semantics; only floating-point channels can interpolate linearly. The
parsers memory-map native files and table functions produce vectorized
DuckDB output.

extensions.name: mpduck
extensions.description: Read and write FIS Prophet files (.rpt, .prn, .fac)

docs.extended_description:
mpduck is a DuckDB extension for reading and writing FIS Prophet files in
`.rpt`, `.prn`, and `.fac` formats, enabling data interchange for actuarial workflows.

extensions.name: mssql
extensions.description: Connect DuckDB to Microsoft SQL Server via native TDS (including TLS).

docs.extended_description:
DuckDB connector for Microsoft SQL Server, Azure SQL and Microsoft Fabric
over a native TDS 7.4 implementation — no ODBC, JDBC or FreeTDS required.
Attach a server as a DuckDB catalog and query, join, and bulk-load it
alongside your local data.

Documentation: https://hugr-lab.com/docs/mssql-extension/

**Reading.** Attached tables come with schema/table catalog integration
and a lazily loaded metadata cache. A SELECT the extension can write in
T-SQL — joins, aggregates, GROUP BY, window functions, ORDER BY / LIMIT,
subqueries, CTEs — runs on SQL Server as one statement (EXPLAIN shows it);
the rest streams through projection and filter pushdown and a columnar,
batch-decoded result path.

**Writing.** COPY TO, CTAS and large INSERTs ship over the BCP bulk-load
protocol with up to 8 parallel sessions. UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT … SELECT
and MERGE run on the server as one statement when they can be written in
T-SQL, and through a session staging table otherwise — no primary key
required, RETURNING supported. DuckDB transactions map to SQL Server
transactions on one pinned connection.

**Authentication and security.** SQL logins, Azure Entra ID (Service
Principal, CLI, Device Code), Kerberos on POSIX, Windows SSPI, DuckDB
secrets; TLS with the server certificate verified by default.

**Operations.** Per-catalog connection pooling, eager ATTACH-time
credential validation, named-instance resolution via SQL Server Browser,
custom Application Name.

Issues and feature requests: https://github.com/hugr-lab/mssql-extension

extensions.name: mssql_ducklake
extensions.description: DuckLake with its catalog in Microsoft SQL Server or Azure SQL - embedded DuckLake, native TDS through the mssql extension.

docs.extended_description:
Runs [DuckLake](https://ducklake.select) with its **catalog in Microsoft SQL Server or Azure SQL**. The extension embeds the complete, unmodified DuckLake source at a pinned commit (catalog format 1.1 on DuckDB 2.0) and adds a SQL Server metadata manager beside DuckLake's built-in PostgreSQL and SQLite ones; it talks to the server through the mssql extension (native TDS, no ODBC), which must be installed too. Everything DuckLake does - snapshots, time travel, schema evolution, data inlining, partitioning, the maintenance functions, `ducklake:postgres:` catalogs as well - works as in the stock extension; the data files live wherever DuckLake puts them.

Documentation: https://hugr-lab.com/docs/mssql-ducklake/

**Mutually exclusive with the stock `ducklake` extension**: both provide the same functions and the same `ducklake:` attach prefix - load one or the other, and load `mssql_ducklake` before the first `ATTACH 'ducklake:...'`. Needs the mssql extension (v0.3.0 or newer on DuckDB 2.0, v0.2.5 or newer on 1.5.6), and a SQL Server 2019+ or Azure SQL database (a UTF-8 collation).

Experimental. The catalog is shaped for SQL Server on creation (primary keys, UTF-8 binary collation, indexes, forced parameterization), a commit goes to the server as one T-SQL batch, and the catalog loads in one statement and is kept per ATTACH. On equal Azure VMs the 500-table benchmark takes 0.63x of the PostgreSQL backend's time; what is not there yet is on the limitations page.

extensions.name: nanoarrow
extensions.description: Allows the consumption and production of the Apache Arrow interprocess communication (IPC) format, both from files and directly from stream buffers.

docs.extended_description:
The Arrow IPC library allows users to read and write data in the Arrow IPC stream format.
This can be done by either reading and producing `.arrow` files or by directly reading buffers using their pointers and sizes.
It is important to note that reading buffers is dangerous, as an incorrect pointer can crash the database system.
This process is temporary and will be deprecated in the future, as clients (e.g., the Python DuckDB client) will have a function that internally extracts these buffers from an Arrow stream.

extensions.name: nats_js
extensions.description: Query NATS JetStream message streams directly with SQL

docs.extended_description:
The nats_js extension reads the messages stored in NATS JetStream streams with SQL. It creates no consumers.

Features:
- Subject filters with NATS wildcards, applied by the server
- Sequence ranges (start_seq, end_seq) and time ranges (start_time, end_time), also from WHERE clauses
- Batched reads on nats-server 2.11 and later
- Message headers as a MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR[]) column
- JSON field extraction with dot paths for nested fields
- Protocol Buffers decoding from a .proto file at query time, with native DuckDB types
- Authentication and TLS through DuckDB secrets of type nats
- Streams with or without allow_direct

Documentation: https://github.com/brannn/duckdb-nats-jetstream

extensions.name: netquack
extensions.description: DuckDB extension for parsing, extracting, and analyzing domains, URIs, and paths with ease.

docs.extended_description:
This extension designed to simplify working with domains, URIs, IPs, and web paths directly within your database queries. Whether you're extracting top-level domains (TLDs), parsing URI components, or analyzing web paths, Netquack provides a suite of intuitive functions to handle all your network tasks efficiently. Built for data engineers, analysts, and developers.

With Netquack, you can unlock deeper insights from your web-related datasets without the need for external tools or complex workflows.

Check the [documentation](https://github.com/hatamiarash7/duckdb-netquack) for more details and examples on each function.

extensions.name: ng_postcode
extensions.description: Parse, validate, format, and group Nigeria's NIPOST digital postcode (NDAPS)

docs.hello_world:
SELECT ng_postcode_parse('ek 01 a03 fk 01') AS code,
       ng_postcode_format(ng_postcode_truncate('ek 01 a03 fk 01', 'district')) AS district;
docs.extended_description:
Nigeria's digital postcode has eleven letters and digits in five segments: state, local government area, district, area, and unit. It is written `EK-01-A03-FK-01` and stored as `EK01A03FK01`.

This extension reads the code offline, with no network call and no lookup table. A value that is not a well-formed code gives NULL.

- `ng_postcode_parse(text)` returns the compact form of a complete code.
- `ng_postcode_prefix_parse(text)` accepts a code cut off after any segment.
- `ng_postcode_format(text)` returns the hyphenated form.
- `ng_postcode_truncate(text, segment)` cuts a code after `state`, `lga`, `district`, `area`, or `unit`.
- `ng_postcode_parent(text)` returns the next coarser prefix.
- `ng_postcode_within(text, prefix)` tells whether a code lies inside a prefix.
- `ng_postcode_compact(text)` strips spaces and hyphens and uppercases.
- `ng_postcode_version()` returns the extension version.

Counting rows by district needs no map:
```sql
SELECT ng_postcode_format(ng_postcode_truncate(postcode, 'district')) AS district, count(*)
FROM deliveries GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
```

The functions pass the shared test cases of the [ng-postcode](https://github.com/Adeniyikayodee/ng-postcode) libraries for Rust, Python, JavaScript, and Java. The source is at https://github.com/Adeniyikayodee/ng-postcode-duckdb.

extensions.name: oast
extensions.description: Validate, decode, and extract OAST (Out-of-Band Application Security Testing) domains in SQL

docs.extended_description:
The oast extension provides functions for working with OAST (Out-of-Band Application Security Testing)
domains directly in SQL. OAST domains are used by security testing tools like ProjectDiscovery Interactsh
to detect out-of-band interactions during vulnerability scanning.

Functions include validation (oast_validate), metadata decoding (oast_struct, oast_decode_json),
domain extraction from text (oast_extract, oast_extract_decode), and convenience macros for
field access (oast_campaign, oast_timestamp, oast_ksort, oast_machine_id).

Supports domains from: oast.pro, oast.live, oast.site, oast.online, oast.fun, oast.me, interact.sh, interactsh.com.

Pure C implementation with no external dependencies. Uses DuckDB stable C API (v1.2.0+).

extensions.name: observefs
extensions.description: Provides IO observability to filesystem

docs.hello_world: COPY (SELECT observefs_get_profile()) TO '/tmp/output.txt';
docs.extended_description:
This extension provides observability to duckdb filesystems.
It supports a few key features:
- 100% compatible with duckdb httpfs
- Record latency for most of the IO operations (open, read, write, etc)
- Provides both process-wise and bucket-wise latency stats (including histogram and quantile estimation) to all read operations
- Provides cache access insight to duckdb external file cache
